claim: MChIP-C is a new MNase-based proximity ligation method that allows measurement of protein-mediated chromatin interactions at single-nucleosome resolution on a genome-wide scale.
source: In this study, we present a new MNase-based proximity ligation method called MChIP-C, allowing for the measurement of protein-mediated chromatin interactions at single-nucleosome resolution on a genome-wide scale.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the development and capabilities of MChIP-C, supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: MChIP-C has greatly improved resolution and sensitivity compared to restriction endonuclease-based C-methods when applied to study H3K4me3 promoter-centered interactions in K562 cells.
source: By applying MChIP-C to study H3K4me3 promoter-centered interactions in K562 cells, we found that it had greatly improved resolution and sensitivity compared to restriction endonuclease-based C-methods.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analyses with PLAC-seq and Hi-C shown in Figures 2 and 4, demonstrating superior signal-to-noise ratios and interaction detection rates.

claim: EP300 histone acetyltransferase and the SWI/SNF remodeling complex are potential candidates for establishing and/or maintaining enhancer-promoter interactions.
source: This allowed us to identify EP300 histone acetyltransferase and the SWI/SNF remodeling complex as potential candidates for establishing and/or maintaining enhancer-promoter interactions.
evidence: The claim is supported by random forest modeling showing EP300 and SWI/SNF subunits as strong predictors of MChIP-C signal (Figure 3d) and their enrichment in regulatory interactions (Figure 3c).

claim: Most functionally verified enhancers physically interact with their cognate promoters, supporting the enhancer-promoter looping model.
source: Finally, leveraging data from published CRISPRi screens, we found that most functionally verified enhancers do physically interact with their cognate promoters, supporting the enhancer-promoter looping model.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing 60.7% of CRISPRi-verified E-P pairs have underlying spatial interactions in MChIP-C (Figure 4a), compared to only 6.5% of non-regulatory pairs.

claim: The enhancer-promoter looping model, in which enhancers activate their target genes via physical contact, has long dominated the field of gene regulation.
source: For decades since the discovery of the first enhancers, the enhancer-promoter (E-P) looping model, in which enhancers activate their target genes via physical contact, has dominated the field (Popay and Dixon, 2022; Ptashne, 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature on the E-P looping model.

claim: Direct empirical evidence for the enhancer-promoter looping hypothesis has been scarce, with only a handful of credible enhancers demonstrated to be in physical proximity to their promoter partners.
source: However, direct empirical evidence for this hypothesis has been scarce, and only a handful of credible enhancers were demonstrated to be in physical proximity to their promoter partners.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to specific examples of validated E-P interactions.

claim: Classical enhancers and their established targets include globin genes, HoxD cluster genes, Shh and PAX6 genes.
source: These include classical enhancers and their established targets such as globin genes, HoxD cluster genes, Shh and PAX6 genes (Tolhuis et al., 2002; Davies et al., 2016; Oudelaar et al., 2019; Hua et al., 2021; Montavon et al., 2011; Symmons et al., 2016; Freire-Pritchett et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies demonstrating these E-P interactions.

claim: Some recent microscopy observations do not seem to align well with the E-P looping model.
source: Simultaneously, some recent microscopy observations do not seem to align well with the E-P looping model (Benabdallah et al., 2019; Karr et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to microscopy studies that challenge the E-P looping model.

claim: C-methods have revolutionized the study of genome spatial organization, providing a complementary view to microscopic approaches.
source: The development of genomic assays based on proximity-ligation of chromatin, commonly known as C-methods (Cullen et al., 1993; Dekker et al., 2002; Denker and de Laat, 2016), has revolutionized the study of genome spatial organization, providing a complementary view to microscopic approaches (Denker and de Laat, 2016; McCord et al., 2020; Jerkovic and Cavalli, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to foundational and review papers on C-methods.

claim: Genome-wide C-methods have been instrumental in defining salient structural features of mammalian chromatin, including genomic compartments, topologically associating domains (TADs) and cohesin-dependent CTCF point interactions.
source: Both the resolution and throughput of genome-wide C-methods were instrumental in defining salient structural features of mammalian chromatin, including genomic compartments, topologically associating domains (TADs) and cohesin-dependent CTCF point interactions (Lieberman-Aiden et al., 2009; Nora et al., 2012; Sexton et al., 2012; Dixon et al., 2012; Rao et al., 2014; Rowley and Corces, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to landmark studies that identified these chromatin features using C-methods.

claim: Very few specific E-P interactions were observed with conventional restriction enzyme-based C-methods, unlike CTCF-based interactions.
source: However, unlike CTCF-based interactions, very few specific E-P interactions were observed with conventional restriction enzyme-based C-methods.
evidence: The claim is based on the general observation from the field that restriction enzyme-based methods have limited sensitivity for E-P interactions.

claim: Sequencing depth inherently limited the resolution of all vs all approaches such as Hi-C.
source: Initially, sequencing depth inherently limited the resolution of all vs all approaches such as Hi-C, and thus a number of targeted approaches were developed.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the technical limitations of Hi-C.

claim: Targeted C-methods use in-solution hybridization (CaptureC, CaptureHi-C) or immunoprecipitation (ChIA-PET, HiChIP, PLAC-seq) to enrich for interactions of specific regions of interest.
source: In-solution hybridization (CaptureC, CaptureHi-C) or immunoprecipitation (ChIA-PET, HiChIP, PLAC-seq) are exploited in these methods to enrich for interactions of specific regions of interest, thus decreasing the sequencing burden and allowing higher resolution (Hughes et al., 2014; Mifsud et al., 2015; Fullwood et al., 2009; Mumbach et al., 2016; Fang et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to papers describing these targeted C-methods.

claim: Targeted methods revealed a statistical preference of promoters to interact with enhancer-like regions and enabled detection of some individual E-P interactions.
source: While targeted methods clearly revealed a statistical preference of promoters to interact with enhancer-like regions and enabled detection of some individual E-P interactions, in some cases functionally verified enhancers did not show spatial proximity to the promoters of their targets as measured with C-methods (Gupta et al., 2017; Benabdallah et al., 2019), raising further questions concerning the universality and functional relevance of E-P looping.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies using targeted C-methods, while also noting limitations.

claim: In some cases, functionally verified enhancers did not show spatial proximity to the promoters of their targets as measured with C-methods, raising questions about the universality and functional relevance of E-P looping.
source: While targeted methods clearly revealed a statistical preference of promoters to interact with enhancer-like regions and enabled detection of some individual E-P interactions, in some cases functionally verified enhancers did not show spatial proximity to the promoters of their targets as measured with C-methods (Gupta et al., 2017; Benabdallah et al., 2019), raising further questions concerning the universality and functional relevance of E-P looping.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies that found discrepancies between functional and spatial E-P relationships.

claim: The resolution of C-methods based on restriction endonuclease digestion cannot overcome the inherent restriction fragment length limitation.
source: Although targeted methods have circumvented sequencing-depth limitations, the resolution of C-methods based on restriction endonuclease digestion cannot overcome the inherent restriction fragment length limitation, which often results in a high level of background noise and the inability to distinguish CTCF-based interactions from other types of chromatin spatial interactions (Goel and Hansen, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a review discussing limitations of restriction enzyme-based C-methods.

claim: MNase-based C-methods, such as Micro-C and its targeted counterparts (MCC, Tiled-MCC, and RCMC), reduced the resolution limitation, allowing finer chromatin structures to be distinguished.
source: The introduction of MNase-based C-methods, such as Micro-C and its targeted oligonucleotide hybridization-based counterparts, MCC, Tiled-MCC, and RCMC, reduced the resolution limitation, allowing finer chromatin structures to be distinguished (Hsieh et al., 2020; Krietenstein et al., 2020; Hua et al., 2021; Aljahani et al., 2022; Goel et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to papers describing MNase-based C-methods.

claim: The usage of MNase allowed milder detergent pretreatment of crosslinked cells, increasing the sensitivity of Micro-C, MCC and related techniques by retaining E-P interactions.
source: Crucially, the usage of MNase also allowed milder detergent pretreatment of crosslinked cells, increasing the sensitivity of Micro-C, MCC and related techniques by retaining E-P interactions, which appear to be more susceptible to experimental conditions than CTCF-based chromatin interactions (Canver et al., 2015; Fulco et al., 2016; Gasperini et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies showing that E-P interactions are sensitive to experimental conditions.

claim: E-P interactions appear to be more susceptible to experimental conditions than CTCF-based chromatin interactions.
source: Crucially, the usage of MNase also allowed milder detergent pretreatment of crosslinked cells, increasing the sensitivity of Micro-C, MCC and related techniques by retaining E-P interactions, which appear to be more susceptible to experimental conditions than CTCF-based chromatin interactions (Canver et al., 2015; Fulco et al., 2016; Gasperini et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating differential sensitivity of interaction types to experimental conditions.

claim: The development of genomic and epigenomic CRISPR-based functional screens has greatly expanded the amount of available data on functional E-P interactions.
source: In parallel, the development of genomic and epigenomic CRISPR-based functional screens has greatly expanded the amount of available data on functional E-P interactions.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge about the impact of CRISPR screens on the field.

claim: MChIP-C combines the genome-wide throughput of HiChIP with the exceptional resolution and sensitivity of MCC.
source: We developed MChIP-C, a novel MNase-based proximity ligation technique which combines the genome-wide throughput of HiChIP with the exceptional resolution and sensitivity of MCC (Figure 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental design and comparative analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: The MChIP-C protocol starts similar to MCC, where cells are crosslinked with formaldehyde and permeabilized with digitonin.
source: The protocol starts similar to MCC, where cells are crosslinked with formaldehyde and permeabilized with digitonin.
evidence: The claim is supported by the detailed Methods section describing the experimental procedure.

claim: Milder cell permeabilization procedure has been shown to provide higher sensitivity for detecting E-P interactions.
source: This milder cell permeabilization procedure has been shown to provide higher sensitivity for detecting E-P interactions (Hua et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study demonstrating the benefits of mild permeabilization.

claim: MChIP-C avoids using biotin to enrich for ligated fragments, potentially increasing library complexity.
source: As in MCC, we avoided using biotin to enrich for ligated fragments, potentially increasing library complexity, but also resulting in a low proportion of informative chimeric read pairs in the sequencing libraries.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental design choice described in the manuscript.

claim: Four biological replicates of MChIP-C experiment on K562 cells using anti-H3K4me3 antibodies were performed.
source: We performed four biological replicates of MChIP-C experiment on K562 cells using anti-H3K4me3 antibodies to focus on spatial interactions of active promoters.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and supported by the Methods section.

claim: The MChIP-C libraries were paired-end sequenced with a total of ~3.5 B read pairs, yielding ~3 B uniquely mapped reads.
source: The MChIP-C libraries were paired-end sequenced with a total of ~3.5 B read pairs, yielding ~3 B uniquely mapped reads (Figure 1b; Figure 1—figure supplement 1b; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing statistics presented in the manuscript and supplementary materials.

claim: Approximately 91.5% of uniquely mapped reads mapped within 1 kb of each other and approximately 4% mapped further than 5 kb away from each other.
source: ~91.5% (~2.77 B) of these mapped within 1 kb of each other and ~4% (~120 M) mapped further than 5 kb away from each other.
evidence: The claim is supported by mapping statistics from the data analysis.

claim: The 4% fraction of informative reads in MChIP-C was low relative to restriction enzyme-based C-methods but comparable to MCC.
source: While the 4% fraction of informative reads was low relative to restriction enzyme-based C-methods (e.g. >60% informative reads in PLAC-seq), it is comparable to MCC (0.5–5% informative reads, see Methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with published data on other C-methods.

claim: MChIP-C H3K4me3 occupancy profiles of replicates were highly similar (Pearson correlation 0.95–0.97) and match standard H3K4me3 ChIP-seq (Pearson correlation 0.90–0.92).
source: We found that the profiles of replicates were highly similar (Pearson correlation 0.95–0.97) and match standard H3K4me3 ChIP-seq (Pearson correlation 0.90–0.92; Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: 11,743 consensus H3K4me3 peaks were identified amongst MChIP-C replicates.
source: Next, we identified 11,743 consensus peaks amongst replicates and found these mostly colocalized with active RNA polymerase II TSSs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by peak calling analysis described in the Results and Methods sections.

claim: MChIP-C consensus peaks mostly colocalized with active RNA polymerase II TSSs.
source: Next, we identified 11,743 consensus peaks amongst replicates and found these mostly colocalized with active RNA polymerase II TSSs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis with CAGE data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1e.

claim: Single-nucleosome resolution interaction profiles were obtained for 10,955 active promoters after filtering low-coverage viewpoints.
source: Both viewpoint-specific and merged MChIP-C correlated well between replicates (Pearson correlation 0.83–0.92 for merged profiles and 0.62–0.75 for viewpoint-separated profiles; Figure 1—figure supplement 1f), and therefore we combined all replicates, resulting in single-nucleosome resolution interaction profiles for 10,955 active promoters, after filtering low-coverage viewpoints.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data processing pipeline and correlation analysis.

claim: MChIP-C profiles demonstrate that promoters interact with each other and with non-promoter regions.
source: The obtained interaction profiles demonstrate that promoters interact with each other and with non-promoter regions (Figure 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by visual inspection of interaction profiles shown in Figure 1b.

claim: 70–87% of interactions identified in each MChIP-C replicate were present in at least one other replicate.
source: For each of the replicates, we found that 70–87% of its interactions were present in at least one other replicate (corresponding to the amount of sequencing per replicate; see Methods), suggesting that called interactions were generally reproducible.
evidence: The claim is supported by reproducibility analysis of interaction calling across replicates.

claim: 112,087 promoter-promoter (P-P) interactions and 128,986 promoter-nonpromoter (P-PIR) interactions were detected in MChIP-C.
source: Overall, we detected 112,087 promoter-promoter bin (P-P) interactions and 128,986 promoter-nonpromoter bin interactions (Figure 1c; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by interaction calling results presented in Figure 1c and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Both P-P and P-PIR interactions were mostly localized within TADs.
source: Both types of interactions were mostly localized within TADs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of interaction positions relative to TAD boundaries shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1h.

claim: 128,986 promoter-nonpromoter interactions link 10,721 viewpoints with 99,315 unique nonpromoter bins (PIRs).
source: We excluded P-P interactions from subsequent analyses and focused on 128,986 promoter-nonpromoter interactions linking 10,721 viewpoints with 99,315 unique nonpromoter bins (Supplementary file 1) which we refer to as PIRs (Promoter Interacting Regions).
evidence: The claim is supported by the interaction dataset described in the Results section.

claim: MChIP-C profiles showed clear highly-localized interaction peaks corresponding to CTCF-bound sites and enhancers known to control the expression of MYC, GATA1, HBG2, MYB, and VEGFA genes.
source: We found that MChIP-C profiles showed clear highly-localized interaction peaks corresponding to the CTCF-bound sites and enhancers known to control the expression of these genes (Figure 2a; Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by visual comparison of MChIP-C profiles with known regulatory elements shown in Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The MYC gene has seven well-characterized K562-specific enhancer elements (e1-e7) spread along the 2 Mb region downstream of the gene.
source: For instance, the MYC gene has seven well-characterized K562-specific enhancer elements (e1-e7) spread along the 2 Mb region downstream of the gene and MChIPC allowed detection of interactions between MYC promoter and five of these sites.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about MYC enhancers and is supported by MChIP-C data showing interactions with these sites.

claim: MChIP-C allowed detection of interactions between MYC promoter and five of the seven characterized enhancer sites.
source: For instance, the MYC gene has seven well-characterized K562-specific enhancer elements (e1-e7) spread along the 2 Mb region downstream of the gene and MChIPC allowed detection of interactions between MYC promoter and five of these sites.
evidence: The claim is supported by MChIP-C interaction data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: PLAC-seq profiles are much noisier than MChIP-C and lack clear peaks corresponding to either CTCF sites or known enhancers of the interrogated genes.
source: PLAC-seq profiles are by contrast much noisier and lack clear peaks corresponding to either CTCF sites or known enhancers of the interrogated genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by visual comparison of PLAC-seq and MChIP-C profiles shown in Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Micro-C data looks cleaner than PLAC-seq but still misses some interactions that are obvious from MChIP-C data.
source: Interestingly, while the Micro-C data also looks cleaner than PLAC-seq, it still misses some interactions which are obvious from the MChIP-C data.
evidence: The claim is supported by visual comparison of Micro-C and MChIP-C profiles shown in Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: MChIP-C shows a 2.66 median fold enrichment of DHS centers relative to 5 kb background.
source: To quantify this, we compared the MChIP-C signal at DHS centers to MChIP-C "background" signal within 1–5 kb of the DHS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b), and found a 2.66 median fold enrichment of DHS centers relative to 5 kb background (3.23 with CTCF, and 2.07 without CTCF).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of MChIP-C signal at DHSs shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: PLAC-seq shows a very weak enrichment of interactions at DHSs (1.25 median fold enrichment with CTCF and 1.33 without CTCF).
source: In contrast, we found that PLAC-seq shows a very weak enrichment of interactions at DHSs, even for those bound by CTCF (1.25 median fold enrichment with CTCF and 1.33 without CTCF).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of PLAC-seq signal at DHSs shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Micro-C shows a reduced signal-to-noise ratio at DHSs compared to MChIP-C (1.51 median fold enrichment with CTCF and 1.37 without CTCF).
source: Although better than PLAC-Seq, Micro-C shows a reduced signal-to-noise ratio at DHSs compared to MChIP-C (1.51 median fold enrichment with CTCF and 1.37 without CTCF).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of Micro-C signal at DHSs shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: MChIP-C shows better sensitivity and resolution not only on consensus sites but also on sites which were not called as interactions.
source: Remarkably, MChIP-C shows better sensitivity and resolution not only on the consensus sites but also on sites which we failed to call, suggesting that additional interactions could be discoverable by improving the interaction-calling strategy.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of method-specific and consensus interaction sites shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: MChIP-C achieves superior sensitivity and resolution compared to C-methods based on standard restriction enzymes.
source: Thus, in line with other recent reports on MNase-based C-methods (Hsieh et al., 2020; Krietenstein et al., 2020; Hua et al., 2021; Aljahani et al., 2022; Goel et al., 2022; Ramasamy et al., 2022), our results suggest that MChIP-C achieves superior sensitivity and resolution compared to C-methods based on standard restriction enzymes.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analyses with PLAC-seq and Hi-C, and is consistent with published reports on MNase-based methods.

claim: In the context of promoter-centered interactions, MChIP-C outperforms standard whole-genome Micro-C.
source: Additionally, in the context of promoter-centered interactions, our results suggest that MChIP-C also outperforms standard whole-genome Micro-C.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analyses with Micro-C shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: About half of the identified promoter-CTCF interactions (19,773 out of 38,271) showed CTCF binding at the promoter side as well.
source: About half of the identified promoter-CTCF interactions (19,773 out of 38,271) showed CTCF binding at the promoter side as well.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of CTCF binding at both ends of promoter-CTCF interactions.

claim: Only 540 (~2.7%) of promoter-CTCF interactions with CTCF binding on both sides directly correspond to CTCF-CTCF loops reported in a previous Hi-C study.
source: Interestingly, only 540 (~2.7%) of those directly correspond to CTCF-CTCF loops reported in a previous Hi-C study (Rao et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with published Hi-C loop data from Rao et al., 2014.

claim: Promoters preferentially interact with CTCF-bound sites if CTCF motifs are oriented towards the promoter (79% towards vs 21% away).
source: We found that promoters preferentially interact with CTCF-bound sites if CTCF motifs are oriented towards the promoter (79% towards vs 21% away) (Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of CTCF motif orientation in PIRs shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The CTCF orientation bias holds true regardless of the position of the CTCF site relative to the transcription direction (80% vs 20% for upstream CTCF sites and 79% vs 21% for downstream sites).
source: This bias holds true regardless of the position of the CTCF site relative to the transcription direction (80% vs 20% for upstream CTCF sites and 79% vs 21% for downstream sites).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of CTCF motif orientation stratified by position relative to the promoter.

claim: The CTCF orientation bias is observed regardless of CTCF binding at the promoter side.
source: We conclude that interactions of promoters with CTCF-bound sites are biased by CTCF orientation, regardless of CTCF binding at the promoter side.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The CTCF orientation bias suggests the possible involvement of loop extrusion.
source: This orientation bias suggests the possible involvement of loop extrusion.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed CTCF orientation bias and knowledge of loop extrusion mechanisms.

claim: Most of the analyzed transcription-related factors and histone post-translational modifications are substantially enriched in MChIP-C PIRs (4–25 X).
source: Most of the analyzed transcription-related factors and histone post-translational modifications are substantially enriched in MChIP-C PIRs (4–25 X; Figure 3b; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by enrichment analysis of 271 ChIP-seq profiles in PIRs shown in Figure 3b.

claim: H3K27me3 is not enriched in MChIP-C PIRs (1137 overlaps, 1953 [SD = 44] expected by chance).
source: Notable exceptions are facultative heterochromatin-associated histone mark H3K27me3 (1137 overlaps, 1953 [SD = 44] expected by chance) and LINE1-binding protein ZNF146 (183 overlaps, 180 [SD = 12] expected by chance).
evidence: The claim is supported by enrichment analysis comparing observed vs expected overlaps.

claim: CTCF, RAD21, and SMC3 are among the most highly enriched factors in MChIP-C PIRs.
source: As expected, CTCF (22,943/1679 [SD = 41]), cohesin subunits RAD21 (10,702/413 [SD = 23]) and SMC3 (12,956/576 [SD = 27]) are among the most highly enriched factors.
evidence: The claim is supported by enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Hierarchical clustering of PIR-overlapping DHSs identified four major clusters based on transcription factor binding profiles.
source: Rather than separately consider each factor associated with a PIR, we next used hierarchical clustering to partition PIR-overlapping DHSs (i.e. promoter interacting DHSs; N=19,129) into groups according to the factor binding profile of each DHS. We identified four major clusters (Figure 3c; Figure 3—figure supplement 2a; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Clusters 1 and 2 DHSs were almost universally bound by CTCF (98.1% and 93.6%), cohesin subunits SMC3 (87.5% and 66.9%) and RAD21 (73.6% and 52.9%), and ZNF143 (87.3% and 66.3%).
source: Clusters 1 (N=4447) and 2 (N=4791) were almost universally bound by the structural factors CTCF (98.1% and 93.6% in clusters 1 and 2 correspondingly), cohesin subunits SMC3 (87.5% and 66.9%) and RAD21 (73.6% and 52.9%) as well as zinc finger protein ZNF143 (87.3% and 66.3%).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of TRF binding in clustered DHSs shown in Figure 3c.

claim: 24,331 interactions with a median distance of ~92 kb were anchored in DHSs from clusters 1 and 2.
source: A total of 24,331 interactions with a median distance of ~92 kb were anchored in DHSs from these two clusters (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of interaction distances for different DHS clusters shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2b.

claim: DHSs from clusters 3 and 4 contained almost no CTCF- or cohesin-bound sites but were enriched in dozens of transcription-related factors.
source: DHSs from clusters 3 (N = 3168) and 4 (N=6723) contained almost no CTCF- or cohesin-bound sites but they were enriched in dozens of transcription-related factors.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of TRF binding in clustered DHSs shown in Figure 3c.

claim: CRISPRi-confirmed enhancers were significantly overrepresented in cluster 3 DHSs (171/297 overlaps; one-sided binomial test, p=1.64*10–57).
source: Notably, CRISPRi-confirmed enhancers (Fulco et al., 2019; Gasperini et al., 2019) were significantly overrepresented in cluster 3 DHSs (171/297 overlaps; one-sided binomial test, p=1.64*10–57), and we thus labeled P-cluster 3 DHS interactions as regulatory interactions.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of enhancer enrichment in cluster 3 DHSs.

claim: There were 7214 regulatory interactions, which tended to be shorter (median length ~47 kb) than structural interactions.
source: Overall, there were 7214 regulatory interactions, which tended to be shorter (median length ~47 kb) than structural ones (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of interaction distances shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2b.

claim: Cohesin subunits were absent in the vast majority of class 3 DHSs, indicating that cohesin may not be involved in the maintenance of regulatory interactions.
source: Interestingly, cohesin subunits were absent in the vast majority of class 3 DHSs. In agreement with a number of recent observations (Thiecke et al., 2020; Hsieh et al., 2022) this may indicate that cohesin is not involved in the maintenance of the regulatory interactions, albeit such a role was suggested earlier (Kagey et al., 2010; Phillips-Cremins et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on the observed absence of cohesin in cluster 3 DHSs and is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: An initial random forest model consisting of genomic distance, CTCF ChIP-seq signal, and motif orientations was able to explain ~37% of variance in the MChIP-C signal.
source: The initial random forest model consisted of five features: DHS-promoter genomic distance, CTCF ChIP-seq signal at both the promoter and the DHS, and motif orientations on both the promoter and the DHS. This initial model was able to explain ~37% of variance in the MChIP-C signal.
evidence: The claim is supported by random forest modeling results shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Adding RAD21 and EP300 to the random forest model increased predictive performance to an R2 of ~43%.
source: Then, we iteratively added the most predictive feature out of a set of 270 ChIP-seq profiles, where predictivity is calculated as R2 in threefold cross-validation. Using this strategy, cohesin subunit RAD21 and histone acetyltransferase EP300 were automatically selected, after which predictive performance plateaued at an R2 of ~43% (Figure 3d).
evidence: The claim is supported by greedy forward feature selection results shown in Figure 3d.

claim: EP300 was threefold enriched in cluster 3 DHSs and 92.2% of cluster 3 DHSs showed EP300 binding.
source: As CTCF and RAD21 are mostly associated with structural loops, we asked whether EP300 mainly underlies regulatory interactions. Indeed, we find that EP300 was threefold enriched in cluster 3 DHSs and 92.2% of cluster 3 DHSs showed EP300 binding.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of EP300 binding in cluster 3 DHSs.

claim: The only proteins that had more binding sites in cluster 3 DHSs than EP300 are subunits of the SWI/SNF remodeling complex: DPF2 (97.8%), ARID1B (95.6%), and SMARCE1 (94.3%).
source: Interestingly, we noticed that the only proteins that had more binding sites in cluster 3 DHSs are subunits of the SWI/SNF remodeling complex: DPF2 (97.8%), ARID1B (95.6%), and SMARCE1 (94.3%; Figure 3c).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of TRF binding in cluster 3 DHSs shown in Figure 3c.

claim: EP300 has been found to directly interact with SWI/SNF-complex.
source: EP300 has been found to directly interact with SWI/SNF-complex (Alver et al., 2017; Blümli et al., 2021) and their chromatin binding profiles are highly correlated (Pearson correlation 0.65–0.70).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating EP300-SWI/SNF interaction and by correlation analysis of their binding profiles.

claim: The chromatin binding profiles of EP300 and SWI/SNF subunits are highly correlated (Pearson correlation 0.65–0.70).
source: EP300 has been found to directly interact with SWI/SNF-complex (Alver et al., 2017; Blümli et al., 2021) and their chromatin binding profiles are highly correlated (Pearson correlation 0.65–0.70).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of ChIP-seq profiles.

claim: The predictive power of SWI/SNF subunits is very close to that of EP300.
source: Revisiting the binding profiles of these SWI/SNF subunits, we found their predictive power to be very close to that of EP300 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: The claim is supported by random forest modeling results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2c.

claim: RNA polymerase II, mediator complex, YY1 and BRD4 are weaker predictors of MChIP-C signal than EP300 and the SWI/SNF subunits.
source: We also specifically examined the predictive power of RNA polymerase II, mediator complex, YY1 and BRD4, which were previously suggested to be associated with enhancer-promoter interaction (Papantonis and Cook, 2011; Kagey et al., 2010; Weintraub et al., 2017; Hnisz et al., 2017), and find that while they individually have some predictive power, they are weaker predictors of MChIP-C signal than EP300 and the SWI/SNF subunits (Figure 3—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: The claim is supported by random forest modeling results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2c and citations to previous studies.

claim: EP300 and/or the SWI/SNF complex might be involved in the formation of regulatory chromatin interactions independently of СTCF and cohesin.
source: Thus, we suggest that EP300 and/or the SWI/SNF complex might be involved in the formation of regulatory chromatin interactions independently of СTCF and cohesin.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the predictive power of EP300 and SWI/SNF in the absence of CTCF/cohesin in regulatory interactions.

claim: 60.7% (222/366, 95% CI [55.7%; 65.7%]) of functionally verified E-P pairs have underlying spatial interactions detected with MChIP-C.
source: Notably, we found that 60.7% (222/366, 95% CI [55.7%; 65.7%]) of the verified pairs have underlying spatial interactions detected with MChIP-C, while only 6.5% (3,554/54,811, 95% CI [6.3%; 6.7%]) of non-regulatory DHS-P pairs show such interactions (Figure 4a and b; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of MChIP-C interactions with CRISPRi-validated E-P pairs shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Only 6.5% (3,554/54,811, 95% CI [6.3%; 6.7%]) of non-regulatory DHS-P pairs show spatial interactions in MChIP-C.
source: Notably, we found that 60.7% (222/366, 95% CI [55.7%; 65.7%]) of the verified pairs have underlying spatial interactions detected with MChIP-C, while only 6.5% (3,554/54,811, 95% CI [6.3%; 6.7%]) of non-regulatory DHS-P pairs show such interactions (Figure 4a and b; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of MChIP-C interactions with non-functional DHS-P pairs shown in Figure 4a.

claim: A majority of experimentally validated enhancers exhibit interaction with their target promoters.
source: Thus, we conclude that a majority of experimentally validated enhancers exhibit interaction with their target promoters.
evidence: The claim is based on the finding that 60.7% of CRISPRi-verified E-P pairs show MChIP-C interactions.

claim: The recall of MChIP-C (60.7%) was superior to those of PLAC-seq (14.0%), Micro-C (19.9%), and Hi-C (2.2%) for detecting CRISPRi-verified E-P pairs.
source: With respect to recall/sensitivity, the recall of MChIP-C (60.7%, as mentioned above) was superior to those of PLAC-seq (14.0%), Micro-C (19.9%), and Hi-C (2.2%).
evidence: The claim is supported by systematic comparison of different C-methods' ability to detect CRISPRi-verified E-P pairs shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The precision of MChIP-C (5.9%) was comparable to PLAC-seq (4.0%), Micro-C (7.4%), and Hi-C (2.4%).
source: In spite of this, the precision of the methods was comparable, with 5.9% for MChIP-C, 4.0% for PLAC-seq, 7.4% for Micro-C, and 2.4% for Hi-C.
evidence: The claim is supported by systematic comparison of different C-methods shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: 50% down-sampled MChIP-C maintains a high recall of 56.1%, with slightly better precision (6.3%) and false positive rate (5.5%).
source: Evaluating predictive performance after down-sampling, we find that 50% down-sampled MChIP-C maintains a high recall of 56.1%, with slightly better precision (6.3%) and false positive rate (5.5%).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of down-sampled MChIP-C data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: At 10% down-sampling, MChIP-C achieves a better precision (10.4%) and false positive rate (1%) than competing methods, while its recall (18.2%) is slightly worse than Micro-C but better than PLAC-Seq and Hi-C.
source: Even at 10% down-sampling, MChIP-C achieves a better precision (10.4%) and false positive rate (1%) than the competing methods, while its recall (18.2%) is slightly worse than that of Micro-C but better than those of PLAC-Seq and Hi-C.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of down-sampled MChIP-C data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The enhanced sensitivity of MChIP-C enables detection of a larger and more precise set of enhancer-promoter interactions than the alternatives.
source: In summary, these results suggest that the enhanced sensitivity of MChIP-C enables detection of a larger and more precise set of enhancer-promoter interactions than the alternatives.
evidence: The claim is based on the comparative analysis of MChIP-C with other C-methods.

claim: In some instances, weak interactions were visually apparent but were missed by the interaction calling algorithm, especially in viewpoints that had low coverage.
source: First, we noticed that, in some instances, weak interactions were visually apparent but were missed by the interaction calling algorithm, especially in viewpoints that had low coverage (Figure 4b, iv).
evidence: The claim is based on visual inspection of MChIP-C profiles for validated E-P pairs without called interactions.

claim: When considering 185/366 validated E-P pairs corresponding to high-coverage viewpoints, 68.1% (126/185, 95% CI [61.4%; 74.8%]) had underlying MChIP-C spatial interactions.
source: Indeed, when we considered 185/366 validated E-P pairs corresponding to high-coverage viewpoints, 68.1% (126/185, 95% CI [61.4%; 74.8%]) had underlying MChIP-C spatial interactions.
evidence: The claim is supported by reanalysis of high-coverage viewpoints.

claim: In some cases, adjacent H3K27ac-positive regions clearly interacting with the expected promoter were observed, possibly suggesting inexact identification of the enhancer position due to the limited resolution of the CRISPRi screens.
source: Second, in some cases we noticed adjacent (few kb) H3K27ac-positive regions clearly interacting with the expected promoter, possibly suggesting inexact identification of the enhancer position due to the limited resolution of the CRISPRi screens (Gasperini et al., 2019; Figure 4b, v).
evidence: The claim is based on visual inspection of MChIP-C profiles and is supported by a citation discussing CRISPRi screen resolution.

claim: CRISPRi-detected E-P interactions are not guaranteed to represent direct effects, as an enhancer may impose secondary influence through the action of the directly targeted gene.
source: Third, CRISPRi-detected E-P interactions are not guaranteed to represent direct effects. In some cases, an enhancer may impose secondary influence through the action of the directly targeted gene (Gasperini et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the CRISPRi study and by a specific example (LMO2-CAT).

claim: The genomic distance between non-interacting E-P pairs (median 71 kb) is substantially larger than between interacting E-P pairs (median 30 kb).
source: Indeed, we observed that the genomic distance between non-interacting E-P pairs (median 71 kb) is substantially larger than between interacting E-P pairs (median 30 kb), supporting the possibility of indirect activation (Figure 4c).
evidence: The claim is supported by distance distribution analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: 59 of 366 verified E-P pairs show CTCF occupancy at enhancer side, and 13 of these lack E-P interaction in MChIP-C.
source: Indeed, 59 of 366 verified E-P pairs show CTCF occupancy at enhancer side, and 13 of these lack E-P interaction in MChIP-C.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of CTCF binding in CRISPRi-verified E-P pairs.

claim: The fraction of verified E-P pairs in which spatial interaction is observed is likely underestimated.
source: In summary, we conclude that the fraction of verified E-P pairs in which we observe a spatial interaction is likely underestimated, which further supports the notion that most enhancers physically interact with their targets and that many such interactions may have not been identified previously due to technical limitations of the employed methods.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the analysis of cases where interactions were missed and the reasons for missing them.

claim: Most enhancers physically interact with their targets and many such interactions may have not been identified previously due to technical limitations of the employed methods.
source: In summary, we conclude that the fraction of verified E-P pairs in which we observe a spatial interaction is likely underestimated, which further supports the notion that most enhancers physically interact with their targets and that many such interactions may have not been identified previously due to technical limitations of the employed methods.
evidence: The claim is based on the high rate of E-P interactions detected by MChIP-C compared to other methods and the analysis of missed interactions.

claim: MChIP-C integrates proximity ligation of MNase-digested chromatin with chromatin immunoprecipitation and deep sequencing.
source: In this study, we present a new high-resolution genome-wide C-method, MChIP-C, which integrates proximity ligation of MNase-digested chromatin with chromatin immunoprecipitation and deep sequencing.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the Discussion and is supported by the Methods section.

claim: MChIP-C allows precise mapping of localized chromatin interactions including E-P contacts which often evade capture by restriction endonuclease-based C-methods.
source: Like other MNase-based C-methods, MChIP-C allows precise mapping of localized chromatin interactions including E-P contacts which often evade capture by restriction endonuclease-based C-methods (Goel and Hansen, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by the comparative analyses with restriction enzyme-based methods and a citation to a review.

claim: MChIP-C uniquely combines the resolution and sensitivity of MCC with the genome-wide scale of Micro-C.
source: Uniquely, MChIP-C combines the resolution and sensitivity of MCC with the genome-wide scale of Micro-C.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental design and comparative analyses showing MChIP-C's advantages.

claim: Tens of thousands of localized spatial interactions between promoters and distal genomic sites were mapped using H3K4me3-directed MChIP-C in K562 cells.
source: Applying H3K4me3-directed MChIP-C to K562 cells, we explored the spatial connectivity of active promoters. Single-nucleosome resolution and high sensitivity allowed us to map tens of thousands of localized spatial interactions between promoters and distal genomic sites.
evidence: The claim is supported by the interaction calling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Previously identified spatial contacts, such as contacts of globin gene promoters with their enhancers, are clearly visible in MChIP-C maps.
source: The quality of the resulting genome-wide profiles is supported by the fact that previously identified spatial contacts, such as contacts of globin gene promoters with their enhancers, are clearly visible.
evidence: The claim is supported by visual inspection of MChIP-C profiles at known E-P interaction loci.

claim: MChIP-C avoids the incorporation of biotin to enrich ligated fragments, thus yielding highly complex libraries.
source: MChIP-C avoids the incorporation of biotin to enrich ligated fragments, thus yielding highly complex libraries.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental design described in the Methods section.

claim: Full realization of MChIP-C potential currently requires a significant sequencing depth due to the small fraction of informative reads.
source: Consequently, full realization of MChIP-C potential currently requires a significant sequencing depth due to the small fraction of informative reads.
evidence: The claim is based on the observation that only ~4% of reads are informative (>5kb apart).

claim: Further experimental optimizations of MChIP-C could significantly increase the method's yield.
source: We anticipate that further experimental optimizations of MChIP-C could significantly increase the method's yield.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about future improvements to the method.

claim: Promoters appear to interact primarily with the surrounding CTCF sites.
source: In agreement with previous observations, promoters appear to interact primarily with the surrounding CTCF sites.
evidence: The claim is supported by the finding that 20.6% of PIRs colocalize with CTCF-bound sites and by citations to previous observations.

claim: CTCF-motifs in promoter-interacting CTCF sites are typically oriented towards the interacting promoter.
source: Interestingly, CTCF-motifs in these sites are typically oriented towards the interacting promoter (Valton et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by the orientation bias analysis shown in Figure 3a and a citation to a related study.

claim: The observed CTCF orientation bias can be explained by the putative ability of active promoters to block movement of the loop extrusion complex.
source: This observation can be explained by the putative ability of active promoters to block movement of the loop extrusion complex which can lead to the establishment of promoter-CTCF loops with CTCF motifs preferentially oriented towards the promoters (Figure 3a, i; Banigan et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is a mechanistic hypothesis supported by a citation to a modeling study.

claim: The observed CTCF orientation bias might be a consequence of architectural stripes, where a CTCF-bound site blocks loop extrusion in a directional manner.
source: Alternatively, the observed bias might be a consequence of a more general phenomenon known as architectural stripes, where a CTCF-bound site blocks loop extrusion in a directional manner, causing nonspecific interactions with an extended nearby region (Vian et al., 2018; which may include the gene promoter; Figure 3a, ii).
evidence: The claim is an alternative mechanistic hypothesis supported by a citation to a study on architectural stripes.

claim: MChIP-C is sensitive enough to identify many relatively weak chromatin interactions that are independent of CTCF binding.
source: Similarly to other MNase-based C-methods, MChIP-C is sensitive enough to identify many relatively weak chromatin interactions that are independent of CTCF binding.
evidence: The claim is supported by the identification of 7214 regulatory interactions in cluster 3 DHSs that lack CTCF binding.

claim: 7214 interactions linking active promoters with distal DHSs bound by a set of enhancer-specific factors were identified.
source: We identified 7214 interactions linking active promoters with distal DHSs bound by a set of enhancer-specific factors.
evidence: The claim is supported by the clustering analysis and interaction calling results.

claim: DHSs in regulatory interactions are highly enriched with functionally verified K562 regulatory sequences and contain chromatin marks typical for active enhancers.
source: These DHSs are highly enriched with functionally verified K562 regulatory sequences and contain chromatin marks typical for active enhancers (Figure 3c; Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by enrichment analysis of CRISPRi-verified enhancers and ChromHMM state analysis shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The increased proximity between promoters and enhancer-like DHSs presumably represents regulatory E-P interactions.
source: The increased proximity between promoters and these enhancer-like DHSs presumably represents regulatory E-P interactions.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the characteristics of cluster 3 DHSs and their interactions.

claim: The E-P looping model assumes that direct physical contact between an enhancer and its target promoter is an essential prerequisite for the promoter activation.
source: One of the long-standing hypotheses explaining enhancer action at a distance is the E-P looping model (Popay and Dixon, 2022; Ptashne, 1986) which assumes that direct physical contact between an enhancer and its target promoter is an essential prerequisite for the promoter activation.
evidence: The claim is based on citations to foundational papers on the E-P looping model.

claim: Technical limitations of methods assessing spatial proximity and scarcity of functional data on mammalian enhancers prevented accurate systematic evaluation of the E-P looping model.
source: Although it is known that at least some enhancers do establish physical contacts with their targets, technical limitations of methods assessing spatial proximity as well as scarcity of functional data on mammalian enhancers prevented accurate systematic evaluation of the E-P looping model.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge about the limitations of previous studies.

claim: The highly dynamic nature of E-P interactions may preclude capturing them with existing proximity ligation techniques.
source: To explain the elusiveness of E-P interactions, it has been suggested that their highly dynamic nature may preclude capturing with existing proximity ligation techniques (Schoenfelder and Fraser, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a review discussing the challenges of detecting E-P interactions.

claim: It is likely that the majority of active enhancers directly interact with target promoters.
source: Thus, it is likely that the majority of active enhancers directly interact with target promoters.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the finding that 60.7% (likely underestimated) of CRISPRi-verified E-P pairs show MChIP-C interactions.

claim: MChIP-C found many apparently non-functional interactions of promoters with DHSs which did not show a significant effect on gene expression in CRISPRi screens.
source: In addition to identifying interactions between promoters and their CRISPRi-validated enhancers, MChIP-C found many more apparently non-functional interactions of promoters with DHSs which did not show a significant effect on gene expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by the finding that 6.5% of non-regulatory DHS-P pairs show MChIP-C interactions.

claim: Non-functional interactions observed in MChIP-C could include structural loops as well as pre-established interactions of promoters with conditionally-activated regulatory elements.
source: Such interactions are also often observed in alternative C-methods, and in some cases could represent CRISPRi false negative pairs. These interactions could also include structural loops as well as pre-established interactions of promoters with conditionally-activated regulatory elements (Jin et al., 2013; Comoglio et al., 2018), and warrant further investigation leveraging the increased sensitivity and resolution of MChIP-C.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the nature of non-functional interactions, supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: It is possible that DNA ends available for ligation can scan a certain territory within fixed nuclei, and thus MChIP-C detected interactions do not exactly represent direct physical contacts.
source: Although it is generally assumed that in the C-methods ligation occurs only between fragments that are in close spatial proximity, the mobility of DNA ends within fixed nuclei has not been extensively studied. It is possible that DNA ends available for ligation can scan a certain territory and thus MChIP-C detected interactions do not exactly represent direct physical contacts.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the technical limitations and interpretation of C-methods.

claim: The data demonstrates that, in most cases, enhancers establish some form of spatial interaction with their targets, resulting in increased ligation frequency.
source: However, we argue that our data demonstrates that, in most cases, enhancers establish some form of spatial interaction with their targets, resulting in increased ligation frequency.
evidence: The claim is based on the high rate of E-P interactions detected by MChIP-C for CRISPRi-verified pairs.

claim: Testing whether spatial interaction is necessary for gene activity would require understanding the physical nature of these interactions.
source: Although we have shown that active mammalian enhancers in general interact with the target promoters, we cannot infer that this interaction is necessary for target activation. Testing whether it is possible to decouple spatial interactions from gene activity would require understanding the physical nature of these interactions.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the limitations of the current study and future research directions.

claim: Various protein factors and physical mechanisms including canonical protein-protein interactions, molecular crowding and liquid-liquid phase separation were implicated in E-P interactions.
source: Various protein factors and a number of physical mechanisms including canonical protein-protein interactions, molecular crowding and liquid-liquid phase separation were implicated in this phenomenon (Kagey et al., 2010; Papantonis and Cook, 2013; Hnisz et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies proposing different mechanisms for E-P interactions.

claim: Cohesin complex was suggested to be involved in E-P interactions, but recent studies exploring cellular responses to acute loss of cohesin found almost no overlap between regulatory E-P interactions and cohesin binding.
source: One protein complex which was suggested to be involved is cohesin (Kagey et al., 2010; Phillips-Cremins et al., 2013). However, in line with studies exploring cellular responses to the acute loss of the cohesin complex (Thiecke et al., 2020; Hsieh et al., 2022), we observed almost no overlap between regulatory E-P interactions and cohesin binding.
evidence: The claim is supported by the observation of cohesin absence in cluster 3 DHSs and citations to recent cohesin depletion studies.

claim: Different groups proposed mediator complex, BRD4, YY1 and RNA polymerase II as candidates for mediating E-P interactions.
source: Different groups proposed other candidates for the role: the mediator complex, BRD4, YY1 and RNA polymerase II (Kagey et al., 2010; Phillips-Cremins et al., 2013; Hnisz et al., 2017; Weintraub et al., 2017; Papantonis and Cook, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies proposing these factors as mediators of E-P interactions.

claim: Recent studies did not identify drastic changes in E-P interaction frequency caused by the degradation or inhibition of mediator, BRD4, YY1, or RNA polymerase II.
source: However, recent studies did not identify drastic changes in E-P interaction frequency caused by the degradation or the inhibition of any of these proteins (Ramasamy et al., 2022; Crump et al., 2021; Hsieh et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent studies testing the role of these factors in E-P interactions.

claim: EP300 and SWI/SNF have rarely been considered as mediators of E-P interaction.
source: Unlike cohesin, mediator, BRD4, YY1 and RNA polymerase II, EP300 and SWI/SNF have rarely been considered as mediators of E-P interaction.
evidence: The claim is based on a review of the literature on E-P interaction mechanisms.

claim: EP300 and SWI/SNF consistently outperformed other enhancer-associated factors in terms of predictive power for MChIP-C signal.
source: However, in our analysis, they consistently outperformed other enhancer-associated factors in terms of predictive power.
evidence: The claim is supported by the random forest modeling results shown in Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 2c.

claim: The potential role of EP300 and SWI/SNF in E-P interaction warrants further experimental exploration.
source: Although these results may be affected by differences in the quality of the ChIP-seq data, the potential role of EP300 and SWI/SNF in E-P interaction warrants further experimental exploration.
evidence: The claim is a recommendation for future research based on the findings of the study.

claim: EP300 and SWI/SNF are known as chromatin modifiers rather than structural proteins.
source: Since both EP300 and SWI/SNF are known as chromatin modifiers rather than structural proteins (albeit some studies suggest such a role for EP300 Ma et al., 2021), it is possible that their participation in E-P interaction is indirect.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the functions of EP300 and SWI/SNF, with a citation noting an exception.

claim: It is possible that EP300 and SWI/SNF participation in E-P interaction is indirect.
source: Since both EP300 and SWI/SNF are known as chromatin modifiers rather than structural proteins (albeit some studies suggest such a role for EP300 Ma et al., 2021), it is possible that their participation in E-P interaction is indirect.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the mechanism by which EP300 and SWI/SNF might influence E-P interactions.

claim: H3K27 residue is a well-documented EP300 nucleosomal target.
source: Although H3K27 residue is a well-documented EP300 nucleosomal target (Tie et al., 2009), a recent study identified several other lysine residues localized in H2B N-terminus that are acetylated by EP300 (Weinert et al., 2018; Narita et al., 2022a; Narita et al., 2022b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on EP300 substrate specificity.

claim: A recent study identified several lysine residues localized in H2B N-terminus that are acetylated by EP300.
source: Although H3K27 residue is a well-documented EP300 nucleosomal target (Tie et al., 2009), a recent study identified several other lysine residues localized in H2B N-terminus that are acetylated by EP300 (Weinert et al., 2018; Narita et al., 2022a; Narita et al., 2022b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent studies on EP300 substrate specificity.

claim: H2B N-terminus acetylation marks correlate with enhancer activity more strongly than H3K27ac.
source: These H2B N-terminus acetylation marks correlate with the enhancer activity more strongly than H3K27ac and therefore qualify for being involved in E-P interaction.
evidence: The claim is based on the cited studies showing stronger correlation of H2B acetylation with enhancer activity.

claim: H2B N-terminus acetylation marks qualify for being involved in E-P interaction.
source: These H2B N-terminus acetylation marks correlate with the enhancer activity more strongly than H3K27ac and therefore qualify for being involved in E-P interaction.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the correlation of H2B acetylation with enhancer activity.

claim: 20.6% of PIRs colocalize with CTCF-bound sites.
source: First, we observed that in MChIP-C 20.6% of PIRs colocalize with CTCF-bound sites (Figure 1c; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis of PIRs with CTCF ChIP-seq data.

claim: Both CTCF-bound and CTCF-less DHSs show increased interaction signal relative to background in MChIP-C.
source: We thus separately examined DHSs with and without CTCF, and found that both types of DHSs show increased interaction signal relative to background.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of MChIP-C signal at DHSs shown in Figure 2b.

claim: 50% downsampling of MChIP-C data maintains 76.3% of the detected interactions.
source: We first observe that although the down-sampling suggests our MChIP-C data is not yet saturated by sequencing depth (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c), 50% downsampling still maintains 76.3% of the detected interactions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by downsampling analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1d.
